title: KL Divergence
body:
Extra information needed o encode a message

---

Evan's line is the definition in words, and the formula is the same statement:

$$
D_{KL}(P \,\|\, Q) = \sum_x P(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = H(P,Q) - H(P)
$$

**The excess bits you pay for believing $Q$ when the truth is $P$.** [[Shannon Entropy]] $H(P)$ is
what an optimal code costs; [[Cross-Entropy]] $H(P,Q)$ is what your code costs; this is the gap.
Kullback-Leibler divergence, also called relative entropy.

Three properties, and the third is the one people get wrong:

- **Non-negative.** $D_{KL} \ge 0$ always, and $= 0$ only when $P = Q$ everywhere. You can never do
  better than the truth by being wrong about it. (It follows from Jensen's inequality on the convex
  $-\log$.)
- **Zero exactly when the model is right**, which is what makes it usable as a training objective:
  driving it down is literally driving $Q$ toward $P$.
- **Not a distance.** $D_{KL}(P\|Q) \ne D_{KL}(Q\|P)$ and it fails the triangle inequality, so it
  is not a metric and not a [[Vector Norm]]. "Divergence" is the careful word. The asymmetry is
  meaningful: $D_{KL}(P\|Q)$ takes its expectation over $P$, so it punishes $Q$ heavily for
  assigning low probability where $P$ has mass, and barely notices $Q$ wasting mass where $P$ has
  none.

## Why the loss is cross-entropy instead

This is the quantity you actually want to minimise, since it is zero exactly at a correct model.
But $H(P) $ is fixed by the data and unaffected by the [[Weights]], so

$$
\arg\min_Q D_{KL}(P\|Q) = \arg\min_Q H(P,Q)
$$

and the constant is not worth computing. **The loss is [[Cross-Entropy Loss]]; the thing being
minimised is this.** That is the whole derivation.

## Elsewhere in the vault

It is the natural measure of "how far is my belief from the truth", which is also the shape of a
Bayesian update: see [[Bayes Theorem]] in [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234), where the information gained
by updating a prior to a posterior is a KL divergence between them.
